items.title: Nancy Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: there was this word, this murmur, from Joe Williams and Cannonball, from many of the artists who came through Columbus, Sonny Stitt, just © Fillius Jazz Archive -5- there’s this kid in Columbus.

ctx.x: What a rare commodity — to have a musician, a fine musician, who would step into that role. “I want to be with him.”

That you know would care about you as a person as opposed to being in the “show business” mode. I did not have this great desire to be in show business, so I really needed to know that there was somebody out there who would allow me to be a person and to use the music to enhance, but be a part of, as opposed to just overshadow everything else. And John understood that. We met, his assistant was a young man from Ohio, Chuck Taylor. As I say, I met Cannon on the corner, this is when he and Nat, in fact both he and…

there’s this kid in Columbus. So John was kind of, I just needed to showcase. And when I was ready I came to New York. And within five, I got a job, which was different. I had worked for a minute, you know, other than singing, between high school and college I worked at an insurance company just to make money just to augment that scholarship. Because I didn’t want to put that kind of burden on my parents. But because I was already making a decent wage, I mean I was earning a living as a singer, it was very…

items.title: Nancy Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: How did that word proliferate? Because if you were too busy working to go see them, how . . . ?

We were all working at the same place, pretty much. They knew that Nancy Wilson and Rusty Bryant had kind of established the 502, and if I were not working, I would go see – I saw Sonny Stitt. I remember that. I saw – I think I went to see B. B. King. But the bottom line is, usually, when people came through town, I was performing someplace. But I met Joe Williams. I met Cannon. I met Miles. I remember sitting in with Miles’s band. Bill Evans was the keyboard player then. That was before college, even.
So you didn’t get to go out too much as an audience member, but every once in a while. I think you once told me that you saw Nat Cole at a theater.
